sections.title: What you told us, first
sections.body: You found an unknown substance in your child's backpack last night and got stonewalled when you asked about it. That is a gut-punch moment, and it makes all your other worries feel more real. Right now you do not know what it is, how often it is being used, or who supplied it. For the next few days, treat this as a safety problem to solve, not a mystery to argue about. Keep the substance stored where your child cannot reach it, in a sealed bag or container. If your child seems unusually drowsy, agitated, confused, has trouble breathing, or you suspect recent use, contact emergency medical services or poison control immediately and bring the substance with you. Do not throw it away yet; it is one of the few hard pieces of information you have. We will build from this point with calm, specific steps, not panic.

sections.title: Where you are right now
sections.body: From what you described, you are dealing with a teen who you believe is using substances multiple times each month, mostly around weekends, with friends you already see as risky. You strongly suspect use but have not had an honest conversation about it; instead you are running into secrecy, avoidance, and frequent arguments. You are seriously worried about safety, but you feel unsure how to confront your child, how much to monitor, and whether you are overreacting or underreacting. Consequences and follow-through at home have been inconsistent, your child's daily routine is loose, and your child rarely takes responsibility. Mood changes and emotional withdrawal are clear, and your child barely talks about stress. You and another parent or guardian often disagree on how to respond, and you feel worn down most weeks. Right now there is no clear next-step plan in place, and last night’s discovery in the backpack raised the stakes.

sections.title: Your first three priorities
items: First, steady yourself before doing anything else. You are second‑guessing, worried about long‑term risks, and feeling overwhelmed most weeks. That mix can easily come out as anger, lecturing, or desperate pleading. Over the next 24 hours, focus on sleep, a short walk, and writing down what you are most afraid of and what you want for your child. Use that list to slow yourself down when things heat up: step out of the room, breathe, and come back when you can speak calmly and briefly instead of arguing.

Second, get on the same page with the other parent or guardian before you go back to your child. Set aside one specific time to talk only about this: what you both believe is happening, what the house rules around substances and safety will be, and what rewards and consequences will look like this week if those rules are broken or kept. Even if you disagree on details, agree not to argue about it in front of your child. A clear, united message matters more than getting every detail perfect.

Third, get support for yourself so you are not doing this alone and exhausted. Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group this week and post exactly what you shared here: the unknown substance, the secrecy, the fights, and the inconsistent follow‑through. Listen for what has actually worked for other parents at this level of concern and copy what fits. Use that group to reality‑check your plan, including the rewards and consequences you set, so you are not deciding everything in your own head at 2 a.m.

recommendations.title: Parent Emotional Regulation
recommendations.headline: Steady yourself before you act
recommendations.body: Your responses already show how much you are carrying: frequent worry, second‑guessing, and feeling overwhelmed most weeks. If you go into conversations in that state, your child mainly hears fear and anger, not the message. For the next few days, build a simple routine: when something upsetting happens (like finding something, or your child coming home late), do three things before responding — pause, take a short walk or move to another room, and write down the one or two points you actually need to say. If you feel yourself getting pulled into an argument, say, “I’m getting too heated. I’m taking a break and we’ll finish this later,” and step away. Join the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group to get real‑time ideas on how other parents keep their cool. If your reactions keep turning into shouting or shutdown this week, the next step is to practice specific calm‑conversation techniques from the Essential Workshop "Effective Communication: Building Trust and Engagement with Your Teen".

recommendations.title: Act on what you are seeing
recommendations.headline: Move from suspicion to concrete action
recommendations.body: You now have two strong signals: your own sense that substance use is happening and the unknown substance you found in the backpack. This week is about moving from worrying to acting. With the other parent or guardian, define clear house rules around substances (no use, no substances in the home, no riding in cars with someone who has been using), plus specific rewards for following them and consequences if they are broken. Plan one focused, non‑yelling conversation where you name what you found and state the rules and next steps. Do not get stuck debating whether your child is actually using; hold the line on safety. The Auxiliary Workshop "Intervening When Substance Use is Present: First Steps and Next Steps" will walk you through how to structure this. If your child continues to deny use and you see more signs this week, the next step is to follow through on the pre‑agreed consequence and schedule a professional assessment for substance use.

recommendations.title: Get the adults aligned
recommendations.headline: Get the adults on the same side
recommendations.body: You reported that you and another parent or guardian often disagree on how to respond. That gap makes your child’s world less predictable and gives substances more room. Set up a separate, calm meeting just between the adults, not in front of your child. Compare what each of you is most afraid of, what you think is actually happening, and what you believe the rules should be. Aim for a simple written list: key rules, rewards for following them (screen time, privileges, rides, later curfew) and consequences if they are broken (loss of those same privileges, extra supervision) that both adults will stick to. Use the Essential Workshop "Building a Support Network" to think about which other family members or supports can quietly back this up, and bring questions about sticking together to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group. If disagreements keep spilling out in front of your child this week, the next step is a dedicated co‑parent session just to finalize and write down shared rules and follow‑through.

recommendations.title: Know what you are dealing with
recommendations.headline: Use drug testing to get facts, not to punish
recommendations.body: Right now you are strongly suspecting use but still guessing at which substances and how often. A drug test you give can turn guessing into information. Frame it this way: “We are worried about your safety and need facts so we can help you. This is not a punishment. It is how we decide what happens next.” Decide in advance what the rewards and consequences will be for cooperating versus refusing, and for a clean versus positive test. The Auxiliary Workshop "Drug Testing" explains timing, types of tests, and how to talk about results. Plan this as a structured step after the first serious conversation, not as a surprise or a threat. If your child refuses a test or the test is positive this week, the next step is to increase supervision immediately and schedule an evaluation with a substance use treatment provider.

recommendations.title: When every conversation turns into a fight
recommendations.headline: Turn fights into shorter, calmer talks
recommendations.body: You are having frequent arguments, you feel unsure how to even bring up substance concerns, and your child rarely opens up about stress. That combination closes every door you need right now. This week, change the pattern in two ways. First, keep talks short and focused: one topic at a time, no lectures. Second, front‑load listening: start with, “I’m going to listen for two minutes first. Then I’ll tell you my piece.” If things escalate, end the talk with a clear line: “I care about you too much to just yell. We’re done for now. The rule still stands.” Practice asking about stress in non‑substance moments (“How is school feeling lately — more stressful, less, or the same?”). The Essential Workshop "Effective Communication: Building Trust and Engagement with Your Teen" gives concrete wording and timing ideas. If every attempt still ends in shouting this week, the next step is to move some key messages into calm, written form (text or note) and reduce in‑person debates.

recommendations.title: Make the rules mean something
recommendations.headline: Make rules, rewards, and consequences real again
recommendations.body: You said consequences have been inconsistent, and your child rarely accepts responsibility. That teaches that rules are negotiable. Start by picking just 2–3 priority rules for this week: no substances, basic safety (like check‑ins, curfew), and phone/online limits. For each rule, attach one clear reward for following it and one clear consequence for breaking it. Write them down and share them calmly with your child, after you and the other adult agree. Do not add new consequences in the heat of the moment; just apply what you already wrote. The Auxiliary Workshop "Behavioral Contracts – A Tool for Positive Change" and Auxiliary Workshop "Setting Boundaries with Respect: Discipline Without Punishment" will help you turn this into a simple written agreement. If your child breaks a rule and you feel tempted to let it slide this week, the next step is to deliberately apply the agreed consequence and acknowledge any progress the next time your child chooses the safer behavior.

recommendations.title: When you are not getting straight answers
recommendations.headline: Respond to secrecy with quiet fact‑finding
recommendations.body: You are seeing secrecy and avoidance, and you have already found an unknown substance in the backpack. That means you cannot rely only on what your child tells you right now. You may need to quietly gather more information from physical spaces and devices. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. This is fact‑finding, not a dramatic confrontation. Note dates, what you find, and any patterns (locations, times, names). The Auxiliary Workshop "How and When to Search a Room" gives detailed guidance so this step does not cause more damage than it solves. If you find more substances, paraphernalia, or concerning messages this week, the next step is to tighten supervision (limits on unsupervised time and rides) and tell your child, calmly, that you know more is going on and the plan is shifting to protect safety.

recommendations.title: You cannot do this on empty
recommendations.headline: Protect yourself from burning out
recommendations.body: You reported feeling exhausted, fearful, or overwhelmed most weeks. That level of strain makes it very hard to think clearly, hold boundaries, or show up the way you want. Treat your own support as part of your child’s safety plan, not a luxury. Commit to one concrete support step this week: a friend or family member you can be honest with, a short daily walk, or a set time you are not problem‑solving. Join the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and be direct about what is wearing you down — the secrecy, the arguments, the worry about long‑term consequences. Ask what other parents did when they felt hesitant but knew they needed to act. If you find your sleep, mood, or functioning slipping more this week, the next step is to schedule an appointment for yourself with a therapist or counselor to get support. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

recommendations.title: What is underneath the behaviour
recommendations.headline: Pay attention to mood and what might be underneath the use
recommendations.body: You are seeing clear and frequent mood changes and withdrawal, and your child almost never talks about stress or emotional pain. That is not just background noise; it is often part of why substances start. Make it explicit that you care about how your child is feeling, not just what rules are being broken. Use simple check‑ins: “Your moods seem all over the place lately and you are more shut down. I’m worried you’re carrying a lot.” Offer options besides talking to you — another family member, school counselor, or a therapist. The Auxiliary Workshop "Managing Stress and Pressure – Helping Your Teen Develop Healthy Coping Skills" will help you offer specific alternatives to using. If mood swings, aggression, or withdrawal become more extreme this week, or you hear anything about not wanting to be alive, the next step is to seek an urgent evaluation from a mental health clinician or treatment provider. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

recommendations.title: The people around your child
recommendations.headline: Tackle the pull of risky friends
recommendations.body: You shared that most of your child's friends are concerning to you. That makes substance use more available and more normalized. Instead of only banning people, get curious and clear. Ask neutral questions about what hangs with these friends are like, where they happen, and what "everyone" does there. Set firm rules about settings (no unsupervised late‑night hangouts in certain locations, no parties without an adult present) and attach rewards and consequences to those, not to specific names. Work to keep at least a couple of safer activities or peers in the mix. The Auxiliary Workshop "Understanding and Navigating Peer Pressure" will help you talk about influence without turning it into a fight over specific friends. If your child keeps spending most free time with high‑risk peers this week, the next step is to tighten limits on unsupervised time and increase check‑ins around where, when, and with whom.

recommendations.title: Bring the school in
recommendations.headline: Bring school in as an extra set of eyes
recommendations.body: You feel only lightly supported by school or community professionals right now. Yet school staff see your child for hours a day and often notice changes early. Request a brief meeting or call with a counselor, administrator, or key teacher. You do not need to share every detail, but say you are worried about mood, peer group, and possible substance use, and ask what they are seeing: attendance, grades, behavior, social shifts. Work with them on simple monitoring steps — alerts for missed classes, agreements about calling you if there are concerns. The Auxiliary Workshop "Partnering with Schools for Your Child's Success" and the Essential Workshop "Building a Support Network" will help you think through who at school to bring in and how. If you hear about skipped classes, sleeping in class, or incidents at school this week, the next step is a follow‑up meeting to create a written support and accountability plan.

recommendations.title: The phone and what is on it
recommendations.headline: Treat the phone as part of the substance picture
recommendations.body: You are often unsure where your child is or what they are doing, and most friends worry you. That means the phone and social media are likely key channels for arranging meetups, getting substances, and feeling pressure. This week, make phone and app supervision explicit and tied to safety: explain that, given what you found and what you suspect, phone use now comes with more oversight. Set clear rules for location sharing, who your child can ride with, which apps are allowed, and when the phone is turned in at night, plus rewards for following those rules and consequences for refusing. The Auxiliary Workshop "Understanding the Impact of Social Media on Substance Use and Mental Health" will help you decide where to tighten. If your child refuses location sharing, hides apps, or you see concerning messages this week, the next step is to scale back phone privileges to a simpler device or reduced hours until trust starts to rebuild.

recommendations.title: Put the structure back
recommendations.headline: Rebuild daily structure and remove easy access to substances
recommendations.body: You described an inconsistent daily routine and uncertainty about whether your home really discourages use. Substances thrive in unstructured time and places where they are easy to stash or use unnoticed. Start with basics: regular wake and sleep times, expected mealtimes, and at least one daily check‑in when your child is sober (morning ride, dinner, evening). Make it clear that there are no substances stored or used in the home by anyone, and secure any alcohol, medications, or other substances so your child cannot access them. Shorten stretches of unsupervised time for now. The Auxiliary Workshop "Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine" offers ideas to do this without turning your home into a war zone. If your child repeatedly comes home late, seems intoxicated, or you find more concerning items at home this week, the next step is to increase supervision further and consider adding an outside treatment program to support what you are doing at home. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

sections.title: What to avoid
items: Do not confront your child about the unknown substance in the heat of anger or panic. A late‑night blow‑up, shouting match, or cornering your child when they are already upset will almost guarantee more lying and shutdown. Wait until you are calmer and the other adult is aligned, then have a shorter, more focused talk.

Do not search your child's room, backpack, or phone confrontationally or as a power move. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. Announcing or performing a search in front of your child turns it into a spectacle and escalates the battle between you instead of quietly gathering facts about the substances.

Do not set consequences without matching rewards or change the rules mid‑argument. Saying, “You’re grounded for a month” in the moment but not following through later teaches your child that your limits are negotiable. Decide rules, rewards, and consequences with the other adult in advance and then apply exactly those, no more and no less.

Do not treat every worrying behavior as a referendum on your parenting. Getting lost in guilt or shame can leave you frozen and hesitant when you actually need to take decisive safety steps, like increased supervision or arranging an assessment. Notice the guilt, but keep acting based on your child’s current risk, not on what it says about you.

Do not ignore the mood changes and only chase the substances. If you push hard on use but dismiss clear mood swings, withdrawal, or hints of distress, your child learns that only rule‑breaking matters, not their pain. Make sure some conversations are about how your child is actually doing, even while you hold firm lines on substance use.

sections.title: Your first 72 hours
sections.body:
Day 1:
Start with your own regulation. Take the next 24 hours to sleep, eat, and move your body, even briefly. Write down what you found in the backpack, what you suspect, and your top three safety concerns. Share this with the other parent or guardian, not with your child yet. Schedule a short, specific time with the other adult to talk only about this. Hold off on any big conversations with your child until you can speak calmly without yelling or pleading.

Day 2:
Use this day for information‑gathering and adult alignment. With the other adult, agree on the basic house rules about substances and safety, plus clear rewards and consequences for this week. Secure any substances or medications at home. Quietly check for any other obvious signs: new paraphernalia, changes in sleep, school issues. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. Review the Auxiliary Workshop "Intervening When Substance Use is Present: First Steps and Next Steps" in full, and read basic facts about the substances most common in your area.

Day 3:
Plan and hold the first focused conversation with your child. Choose a calm time when your child is sober. Keep it short: explain that you found the unknown substance, that you are worried about safety, and that new rules are in place. State the rules, the rewards for following them, and the consequences for breaking them. Expect denial or deflection and do not get pulled into debating whether you are "overreacting". End by saying you are on your child’s side against substances and that there will be follow‑up steps, including possible testing, if concerns continue.

sections.title: Days 4 to 7
sections.body:
Over days 4 to 7, act on what you learned in the first conversation and what you see in your child's behavior.

Assume some mix of denial, deflection, or anger. Hold the line you and the other adult agreed to: the rules and the linked rewards and consequences do not change based on your child’s reactions. If your child breaks a safety or substance rule, calmly apply the consequence you already shared (for example, reduced unsupervised time, limited access to the car or rides, changes to phone use) and point out any choices they made that went in the right direction.

If use still seems likely, schedule a drug test you give, framing it as fact‑finding. If your child refuses, follow the consequence you agreed on and step up supervision. If the test is positive or you find more substances, this is the point to seek professional help from a substance use treatment provider or clinician for an assessment and treatment options. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

During this week, also reach out to school (counselor or administrator) to share concerns and ask what they see, and join the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group to get specific advice on what is happening day by day. By the end of day 7, you should have: clearer rules, some monitoring in place, an initial response to any new use, and at least one appointment or plan with an outside helper if concerns remain high.

sections.title: If you are weighing inpatient or residential care
sections.body:
Intensive outpatient and inpatient or residential programs are bigger steps, but they are sometimes the right ones when safety and substance use have moved beyond what home structure alone can handle. Intensive outpatient usually means your child lives at home but attends several treatment sessions each week. Inpatient or residential care means your child lives at a treatment center for a period of time, with structured days focused on safety, sobriety, therapy, and schoolwork.

Families are usually ready to consider these options when there is ongoing use despite clear rules and consequences, repeated findings of substances or paraphernalia, serious safety incidents, or when mood or behavior problems are severe enough that you cannot keep your child safe at home. This decision should be made with a treatment provider, therapist, or other qualified clinician who can assess your child’s specific risks and needs. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

Your immediate next step, if you are even wondering about inpatient, is to schedule a professional assessment and start gathering information about intensive outpatient and residential options, so you are not starting from zero if things escalate.

sections.title: Match the Intervention to the Risk
sections.body: The level of intervention should always match the level of risk. Too much intervention can be as counterproductive as too little. As concerns increase, your response should increase with them; as risk decreases, your response can adjust accordingly. The goal is not to use the strongest intervention available—it is to use the level of intervention that best matches what is actually happening with your child.

sections.title: Taking Care of Yourself
sections.body: Taking care of yourself is not a luxury—it’s a necessity. Whether you need some quiet time, a good workout, or the support of counseling, make space for what helps you stay grounded. When you care for yourself, you will be better able to show up strong, present, and healthy for you and your family.

sections.title: Where this can go
sections.body:
You acted the moment you found that unknown substance — you noticed it, you took it seriously, and you reached out for a plan instead of pretending it was nothing. That matters. It means your child has someone in their corner who is willing to look at the hard thing and still keep thinking clearly.

This will not be fixed in one conversation or one week, but every calm boundary you keep and every small, honest talk you manage changes the ground a little. Remember that you and your child are on the same side; the substance is the problem you are both up against. When the arguments flare, keep coming back to that: “I am doing this because your safety matters more than whether you are mad at me right now.”

Use the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group as real backup, not just a resource you might get to someday. Other parents there have sat exactly where you are sitting. Let their experience shorten the path for you and your child.

sections.title: Protecting the progress
sections.body:
Recovery is a journey—not a single event—and protecting the progress your child has already made is one of the most important responsibilities you have as a parent. While many adolescents go on to achieve lasting recovery, setbacks can occur. A setback does not erase the progress that has been made, and it does not have to become a return to the past.

Preparation is one of your greatest strengths. We encourage you to complete the Auxiliary Workshop "Protecting Recovery: Preventing Relapse and Responding to Setbacks." It will help you recognize early warning signs, respond calmly and effectively if challenges arise, and strengthen your family's plan to protect your child's recovery. We also encourage you to participate in the Protecting Recovery Discussion Group, where parents share experiences, encouragement, and practical insights while supporting one another through the ongoing journey of recovery.

Remember, the purpose of monitoring, supervision, conversations, and appropriate boundaries is not simply to discover what happened or when it happened—but to understand why. Identifying and addressing the underlying reasons for substance use gives your child the greatest opportunity for long-term recovery and a healthy, meaningful future.
